subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 14! In this unit you will master two of the most useful measurement skills in all of mathematics: perimeter and area. Perimeter tells you the distance all the way around the edge of a shape. Area tells you how much flat space is inside a shape. These two ideas look similar at first, but they answer completely different questions, and knowing which one you need is a skill you will use for the rest of your life.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 5 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: This unit is written for self-paced learning. That means you set the speed. Read each explanation slowly, copy every worked example onto your own paper and work it through yourself, and only move on once the idea feels solid. Your AI tutor is available day and night to give you more practice, to explain a step in a fresh way, or to check your working. Your teacher will also meet with you about twice a week to help with anything that still feels difficult.

Keep a pencil, a ruler and some squared paper beside you as you work. Mathematics is not a subject you can learn only by reading – you must do it. Draw the shapes, label the sides, and say each formula out loud as you use it. When you make a mistake, do not worry; a mistake is simply a signpost showing you exactly what to practise next. Every skill in this unit becomes automatic with a little honest practice, and the confidence you build here will carry you into area of triangles, surface area and volume in the years ahead.
Explain the difference between perimeter (distance around) and area (space inside).
Measure and calculate the perimeter of rectangles, squares, triangles and irregular shapes.
Calculate the area of rectangles and squares using length × width.
Calculate the area of a triangle using ½ × base × height.
Find the area and perimeter of compound shapes by splitting or subtracting rectangles.
Estimate the area of an irregular shape by counting whole and part squares.
Choose sensible units and convert between them (cm ↔ m, cm² ↔ m²).
Solve real-world problems involving cost, materials, fencing and flooring.

Use standard units of length, mass and capacity (mm, cm, m, km, g, kg, ml, l), convert between a larger and a smaller unit including answers to one decimal place, and order a set of mixed-unit measurements.
Round a measurement to the nearest whole unit, read and compare readings on different scales, and measure a line accurately to the nearest millimetre.

concepts.title: Understanding Perimeter
concepts.explanation:
Perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside edge of a shape. Picture walking right around the very edge of a football pitch until you arrive back where you started – the total distance you walked is the perimeter. If you were building a fence around a field, the perimeter tells you exactly how much fencing to buy.

Because perimeter is a length, we always measure it in units of length: millimetres (mm), centimetres (cm), metres (m) or kilometres (km). Never in square units – those are only for area. This is one of the first things to fix firmly in your mind: perimeter is measured in plain length units like cm and m.

To find the perimeter of any shape, you simply add up the lengths of all its sides. That rule never fails, and it works for every shape, no matter how strange. For common shapes, though, we have quicker methods. For a rectangle, opposite sides are equal, so the perimeter is length + width + length + width. We write this neatly as Perimeter = 2 × (length + width). For a square, all four sides are equal, so Perimeter = 4 × side length.

Let us work an example. Amina marks out a rectangular vegetable plot that is 5 m long and 3 m wide. Using the rule, Perimeter = 2 × (5 + 3) = 2 × 8 = 16 m. So she needs 16 metres of fencing to go all the way around. Now a square example: a square prayer mat has sides of 4 cm on a small model. Perimeter = 4 × 4 = 16 cm. Notice both answers came out as 16, but one is metres of fence and the other is centimetres of edge – always keep the unit attached to the number.
concepts.example: For an irregular shape, there is no shortcut – you must measure and add every single side. Imagine an L-shaped garden. You carefully measure each edge in turn, working around the outside, and add them all together. The most common slip here is forgetting one of the shorter, hidden sides, so it helps to place a small tick on each side as you count it, making sure every edge is counted exactly once.

concepts.title: Understanding Area
concepts.explanation:
Area is the amount of flat space inside a shape. Think of how much carpet you would need to cover a floor completely, or how much paint to cover a wall. That covering amount is the area. Where perimeter is about the border, area is about the whole surface inside.

Because area measures a flat surface, we always measure it in square units: square centimetres (cm²), square metres (m²) or square kilometres (km²). A square unit is simply a square that is one unit long on each side. So 1 cm² is a square measuring 1 cm by 1 cm, and 1 m² is a square measuring 1 m by 1 m. The little raised 2 in cm² reminds us that area involves two directions – across and up.

Why does length × width give the area? Imagine covering a rectangle with 1 cm squares. If the rectangle is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide, you can fit 6 squares along each row, and there are 4 rows. That is 6 × 4 = 24 little squares, so the area is 24 cm². Counting rows of squares is exactly what multiplication does quickly for us. This is why the rule for a rectangle is Area = length × width.

Let us try a metre example. A room floor in Yusuf's home is 6 m long and 4 m wide. Area = 6 × 4 = 24 m². If carpet is sold by the square metre, he needs 24 square metres to cover the floor. For a square, the length and width are the same, so Area = side × side. If a square tile has sides of 5 cm, its area is 5 × 5 = 25 cm². We sometimes write side × side as side squared, which is where the word squared comes from.
concepts.example: It is worth pausing on the difference between our two ideas, because confusing them is the single most common mistake in this whole topic. Perimeter is a distance and is measured in cm or m. Area is a covering and is measured in cm² or m². If Khadija tells you a table top is 200, you must ask: 200 what? If she means 200 cm of edging tape around it, that is perimeter. If she means 200 cm² of surface to polish, that is area. The unit tells you which idea you are dealing with.

concepts.title: Rectangles and Squares – Putting the Formulas to Work
concepts.explanation:
Rectangles and squares appear everywhere, from a sheet of paper to a football pitch to a floor tile, so being quick and confident with their formulas is a huge advantage. Let us gather the four key formulas in one place and then practise using them carefully.

Rectangle perimeter: P = 2 × (length + width)

Here is the golden habit that keeps you from muddling area and perimeter: before you calculate anything, ask yourself, *am I going around the edge or covering the inside?* If you are going around, you are finding perimeter and adding lengths. If you are covering, you are finding area and multiplying. Write the word Perimeter or Area at the top of your working before you touch a single number.

Let us do a fuller worked example. A rectangular football training pitch is 20 m long and 12 m wide. First the perimeter: P = 2 × (20 + 12) = 2 × 32 = 64 m. That is how far Omar runs if he jogs once around the edge. Now the area: A = 20 × 12 = 240 m². That is how much grass covers the whole pitch. Notice again how the same two numbers give two very different answers, and how the units differ: 64 m for the distance around, but 240 m² for the surface inside.

Sometimes a problem works backwards: you are given the area or perimeter and asked to find a missing side. Suppose a rectangular field has an area of 72 m² and a width of 8 m, and you must find its length. Since area = length × width, we have 72 = length × 8, so length = 72 ÷ 8 = 9 m. Working backwards is just using the same formula in reverse, with division instead of multiplication. The same trick works for a square: if a square has area 64 cm², then its side is the number that multiplies by itself to give 64, which is 8 cm, because 8 × 8 = 64.
concepts.example: One more useful idea: two shapes can have the same area but different perimeters, and the other way around too. A 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle has area 24 cm² and perimeter 20 cm. An 8 cm by 3 cm rectangle also has area 24 cm², but its perimeter is 22 cm. Same area, different perimeter! This surprises many learners, and it is a clear reminder that area and perimeter really are two separate measurements, not two names for the same thing.

concepts.title: Area of a Triangle
concepts.explanation:
Triangles are the next shape to master, and they hide a lovely secret. Take any rectangle and cut it in half from one corner to the opposite corner. You get two matching triangles, and each triangle is exactly half of the rectangle. That is why the area of a triangle is half the area of the rectangle that would fit around it. The formula is Area = ½ × base × height.

Two words need care here. The base is the side you choose to measure along the bottom. The height is the straight up-and-down distance from that base to the top point of the triangle, measured at a right angle to the base – not along a slanting side. Beginners often grab a slanted side by mistake, so always look for the straight vertical distance from the base to the tip.
concepts.example: Let us work an example. A triangular sail on a small model boat has a base of 8 cm and a height of 6 cm. Area = ½ × 8 × 6. A tidy way to calculate this is to multiply the base and height first, 8 × 6 = 48, and then take half: 48 ÷ 2 = 24 cm². So the sail covers 24 square centimetres of cloth. Another example: a triangular garden bed has a base of 10 m and a height of 4 m. Area = ½ × 10 × 4 = ½ × 40 = 20 m².

concepts.title: Compound Shapes
concepts.explanation:
Most real shapes are not simple rectangles. A house floor plan, an L-shaped garden, or a swimming pool with a shallow end is a compound shape – a shape made by joining two or more simple shapes together. The good news is that you already have all the tools you need. The trick is to break the compound shape into simple rectangles, work out each one, and then combine them.

There are two methods for finding the area of a compound shape, and both are worth knowing. The addition method: split the shape into two or more rectangles, find each rectangle's area, and add them together. The subtraction method: imagine the shape as one big rectangle with a smaller rectangle removed, find both areas, and subtract the missing piece.

Let us use a real L-shaped garden. Imagine the garden is like a large 6 m by 5 m rectangle with a 2 m by 2 m square bite taken out of one corner. Using the subtraction method: the big rectangle is 6 × 5 = 30 m², and the missing corner is 2 × 2 = 4 m², so the real area is 30 − 4 = 26 m². Now let us check with the addition method: split the L into two rectangles, one 6 m by 3 m and one 4 m by 2 m. Their areas are 6 × 3 = 18 m² and 4 × 2 = 8 m², and 18 + 8 = 26 m². Both methods agree, which is a lovely way to check your work.

Finding the perimeter of a compound shape needs a careful eye, because some side lengths are not written down and you must work them out first. In the L-shaped garden, going around the outside, the sides are 6 m, 3 m, then a short 2 m step in, then 2 m down, then the 4 m base, and finally the 5 m left side back to the start. Before adding, use the given lengths to find any missing ones: a hidden vertical side must equal 3 + 2 = 5 m to match the tall left side, and a hidden horizontal side must equal 6 − 4 = 2 m. Adding all the outside edges: 6 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 22 m.
concepts.example: The key skill for compound shapes is finding those missing side lengths. Here is the rule that never fails: opposite sides of the whole shape must balance. The lengths sticking up on one side must add to the same total as the tall side opposite them, and the same for the horizontal sides. Always draw the shape, label every length you are given, and then reason out the missing ones before you add or multiply. Rushing straight to the numbers is what causes mistakes here.

concepts.title: Estimating the Area of Irregular Shapes
concepts.explanation:
Not every shape is made of neat rectangles and triangles. The outline of a lake, a leaf, your own hand, or a country on a map is an irregular shape with curved or crooked edges. We cannot use a simple formula for these, but we can estimate the area very well by counting squares.

The method is called counting squares. Place the shape on a grid of squares, where each square is a known size such as 1 cm². Then count in two steps. First, count all the whole squares that lie completely inside the shape. Second, look at the part squares on the edge: if a part looks like about half a square or more, count it as one; if it looks like less than half, do not count it. Add the whole squares and the counted part squares together, and you have a good estimate of the area.

For example, suppose a leaf is drawn on centimetre-squared paper. You count 18 whole squares fully inside the leaf. Around the curved edge you find several part squares; judging them, about 7 of them are half-or-more and so you count them as 7. Your estimate is 18 + 7 = about 25 cm². It is not exact, and that is fine – an estimate is meant to be a sensible close value, not a perfect one. If two people estimate the same leaf, they might get 24 and 26, and both are good answers.
concepts.example: Estimation is not only for curved shapes; it is also a checking tool for every calculation you do. Before working out an exact area, glance at the shape and make a rough guess. If Maryam calculates the area of a room as 400 m² but her estimate was about 20 m², the huge gap warns her that something has gone wrong – most likely a decimal-point slip. Good mathematicians estimate first and calculate second, using the estimate to catch big mistakes. This habit will serve you in every maths topic, not just this one.

concepts.title: Length, Mass and Capacity: Units, Conversion and Ordering
concepts.explanation: Length, mass and capacity all use the same family of standard metric units, and converting between them is easy because everything moves in tens, hundreds and thousands. For length: 10 millimetres (mm) = 1 centimetre (cm), 100 cm = 1 metre (m), and 1000 m = 1 kilometre (km). For mass (how heavy something is): 1000 grams (g) = 1 kilogram (kg). For capacity (how much liquid something holds): 1000 millilitres (ml) = 1 litre (l). To convert from a larger unit to a smaller one, multiply; to convert from a smaller unit to a larger one, divide. Because the metric system is based on tens, hundreds and thousands, many conversions give a decimal answer to one place, for example 350 g = 0.35 kg (dividing by 1000 moves the digits three places) or 1.4 m = 140 cm (multiplying by 100 moves the digits two places). When you must put several measurements in order, first convert them all into the same unit so that you are truly comparing like with like — you cannot tell whether 1.2 m or 85 cm is longer until both are written in the same unit (120 cm and 85 cm). Rounding a measurement to the nearest whole unit works exactly like rounding any other number: look at the part after the decimal point, and round up if it is .5 or more.
concepts.example: A recipe lists ingredients as 750 g of flour, 0.5 kg of sugar and 1250 g of butter. Convert them all to kilograms to put them in order: 750 g = 0.75 kg, 0.5 kg stays as 0.5 kg, and 1250 g = 1.25 kg. Ordered from lightest to heaviest: sugar (0.5 kg), flour (0.75 kg), butter (1.25 kg). A second example: a garden hose is 4.6 m long. Rounded to the nearest whole metre, that is 5 m, because the .6 rounds up.

concepts.title: Reading Scales and Measuring Precisely
concepts.explanation: Rulers, scales and measuring jugs all work the same way: they are number lines, and every mark stands for a fixed jump. Before you read any scale, always check two things — what the biggest labelled numbers are, and how many equal gaps sit between them, because that tells you the value of one small mark. On a kitchen scale marked every 100 g between the 0 g and 1000 g labels, each small mark is worth 100 g, so a pointer resting two marks past the 600 g line shows 800 g. On a measuring jug marked every 50 ml between the 0 ml and 500 ml labels, each small mark is worth 50 ml. Different scales are often drawn with similar-looking gaps for very different real amounts, so always read the labelled numbers rather than guessing from how far apart the marks look — a scale that jumps in 100s can look just like one that jumps in 10s until you check the labels. To measure a line to the nearest millimetre with a ruler, line up the 0 mark exactly with one end of the line, then read the small mm mark closest to the other end; a line ending just past the 63 mm mark and before the 64 mm mark is 63 mm (or 6.3 cm) if it is closer to 63 than to 64, and 64 mm if it is closer to 64.
concepts.example: A measuring jug is marked in lines of 50 ml, labelled every 100 ml (0, 100, 200 …). The water level sits one small mark above the 300 ml label, so the reading is 350 ml. On a different jug marked in lines of 20 ml, a level sitting two small marks above the 300 ml label would only be 340 ml — the same-looking gap gives a different amount, which is exactly why checking a scale's labels before reading it matters.

methods.title: How to solve any area or perimeter problem
methods.example: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 9 m wide. Find its perimeter.
steps: Read: decide whether the problem needs area (covering inside) or perimeter (around the edge).
Write: write the correct formula for the shape.
Substitute: put in the numbers with their units and calculate.

methods.title: How to find the area of a compound shape
methods.example: Find the area of the same 12 m by 9 m garden.
steps: Draw the shape and label every side you are given.
Work out any missing side lengths first.
Either split into rectangles and add, or take a big rectangle and subtract the missing piece.
Add or subtract the areas to get the total.

methods.title: How to estimate the area of an irregular shape
methods.example: A square has an area of 36 cm². What is the length of each side, and what is its perimeter?
steps: Place the shape on a grid of squares of known size.
Count all the whole squares fully inside the shape.
Count each part square that is half-or-more as one whole.
Add the whole and part squares for your estimate.

methods.title: Area of a triangle
methods.example: A triangle has a base of 8 cm and a height of 6 cm. Find its area.
steps: Area = ½ × base × height.
First multiply the base and height: 8 × 6 = 48.
Then take half: 48 ÷ 2 = 24 cm².
The height must be the straight distance from the base to the top point, not a slanting side.

methods.title: Working backwards to a missing side
methods.example: A rectangular field has an area of 84 m² and a width of 7 m. Find its length and perimeter.
steps: Since area = length × width, we have 84 = length × 7, so length = 84 ÷ 7 = 12 m.
Now the perimeter: P = 2 × (12 + 7) = 2 × 19 = 38 m.
Check by multiplying your two side lengths together — length × width should give back the original area, 84.

methods.title: Area of a compound shape
methods.example: An L-shaped room is a large rectangle 10 cm by 6 cm with a 4 cm by 3 cm corner removed. Find its area.
steps: Use the subtraction method.
The big rectangle is 10 × 6 = 60 cm².
The removed corner is 4 × 3 = 12 cm².
So the area is 60 − 12 = 48 cm².

workedExamples.title: Perimeter of a rectangle
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 9 m wide. Find its perimeter.
workedExamples.solution: We are going around the edge, so this is perimeter. P = 2 × (length + width) = 2 × (12 + 9) = 2 × 21 = 42 m. So 42 metres of fencing would go all the way around.

workedExamples.title: Area of a rectangle
workedExamples.prompt: Find the area of the same 12 m by 9 m garden.
workedExamples.solution: We are covering the inside, so this is area. A = length × width = 12 × 9 = 108 m². Notice the answer is in square metres because area covers a surface.

workedExamples.title: Square, working backwards
workedExamples.prompt: A square has an area of 36 cm². What is the length of each side, and what is its perimeter?
workedExamples.solution: For a square, area = side × side. We need the number that multiplies by itself to give 36. Since 6 × 6 = 36, the side is 6 cm. The perimeter is then 4 × 6 = 24 cm.

workedExamples.title: Area of a triangle
workedExamples.prompt: A triangle has a base of 8 cm and a height of 6 cm. Find its area.
workedExamples.solution: Area = ½ × base × height. First multiply the base and height: 8 × 6 = 48. Then take half: 48 ÷ 2 = 24 cm². The height must be the straight distance from the base to the top point, not a slanting side.

workedExamples.title: Working backwards to a missing side
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular field has an area of 84 m² and a width of 7 m. Find its length and perimeter.
workedExamples.solution: Since area = length × width, we have 84 = length × 7, so length = 84 ÷ 7 = 12 m. Now the perimeter: P = 2 × (12 + 7) = 2 × 19 = 38 m.

workedExamples.title: Area of a compound shape
workedExamples.prompt: An L-shaped room is a large rectangle 10 cm by 6 cm with a 4 cm by 3 cm corner removed. Find its area.
workedExamples.solution: Use the subtraction method. The big rectangle is 10 × 6 = 60 cm². The removed corner is 4 × 3 = 12 cm². So the area is 60 − 12 = 48 cm².

workedExamples.title: A cost problem
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular room is 5 m by 4 m. Carpet costs 25 shillings per square metre. How much will it cost to carpet the room?
workedExamples.solution: Carpet covers the floor, so we need area: A = 5 × 4 = 20 m². The cost is 20 × 25 = 500 shillings.

workedExamples.title: An optimisation problem
workedExamples.prompt: You have 24 m of fencing to make a rectangular pen. What dimensions give the largest area?
workedExamples.solution: For a fixed perimeter, a square gives the maximum area. The four equal sides come from 24 ÷ 4 = 6 m. So a 6 m by 6 m square gives the largest area, which is 6 × 6 = 36 m².

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: A square tile has an area of 25 cm². Find the length of one side.
workedExamples.solution: The side length multiplied by itself gives 25. Since 5 × 5 = 25, the side is 5 cm.

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: Convert: a) 2 m² into cm², b) 4.85 m into cm.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: An L-shaped figure is a 10 cm by 6 cm rectangle with a 3 cm by 2 cm corner removed. Find its area.
workedExamples.solution: Use the subtraction method. The big rectangle is 10 × 6 = 60 cm². The removed corner is 3 × 2 = 6 cm². So the area is 60 − 6 = 54 cm².

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: You have 40 m of fencing to make a rectangular pen. What dimensions give the largest area, and what is that area?
workedExamples.solution: For a fixed perimeter, a square gives the maximum area. The four equal sides come from 40 ÷ 4 = 10 m. So a 10 m by 10 m square gives the largest area, which is 10 × 10 = 100 m².

activities.title: Measure Your Own Room
activities.materials: a tape measure or a metre ruler, paper and a pencil.
steps: Measure the length and width of a room or a mat in your home, in metres.
Work out the area using length × width, and write it with the unit m².
Work out the perimeter using 2 × (length + width), and write it with the unit m.
Imagine carpet costs 25 shillings per square metre. How much would it cost to carpet your room?
Keep your measurements – you can compare different rooms and see which has the largest area.

activities.title: Squared-Paper Shapes
activities.materials: squared (grid) paper, a ruler and coloured pencils.
steps: On squared paper, draw three different rectangles that each have a perimeter of 24 cm.
Count the squares inside each rectangle to find its area.
Which rectangle has the largest area? Which has the smallest?
Write down what you notice about the shape with the largest area.
This activity shows that shapes with the same perimeter can have very different areas.

activities.title: The Estimation Game
activities.materials: squared paper, a pencil and a few flat objects (a leaf, your hand, a spoon).
steps: Place an object on the squared paper and draw around its outline.
First estimate the area by eye – write down your guess.
Now count the whole squares inside, then the part squares that are half-or-more.
Compare your count with your first guess. How close were you? Try three objects and see if your estimates improve.

activities.title: Garden Designer Investigation
activities.materials: squared paper, a ruler and coloured pencils.
steps: Design an L-shaped garden on squared paper, letting each square stand for 1 metre.
Split your L-shape into two rectangles and find the area of each, then add them.
Now check your answer using the subtraction method (big rectangle minus the missing corner).
Work out the perimeter by carefully adding every outside edge – do not miss any sides!

activities.title: Fencing and Flooring Challenge (Family Task)
activities.materials: your family, a tape measure and a calculator or paper.
steps: Choose a real space at home or outside, such as a room or a small yard.
Measure it and work out both the area and the perimeter together.
Decide: for new flooring, do you need area or perimeter? For a fence or border, which do you need?
Make up sensible prices per metre and per square metre, and work out the total cost as a family.

activities.title: Triangle Halves
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, scissors and coloured pencils.
steps: Draw a rectangle and work out its area with length × width.
Draw a straight line from one corner to the opposite corner, then cut along it.
You now have two matching triangles. Check that each triangle is exactly half the rectangle's area.
Explain in your own words why the area of a triangle is ½ × base × height.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand the difference between area and perimeter best? What was the trickiest part? Did your estimates get better with practice? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: The Perimeter Formula for Rectangles and Squares
rules.text: To find the perimeter of any shape, you simply add up the lengths of all its sides. That rule never fails, and it works for every shape, no matter how strange. For common shapes, though, we have quicker methods. For a rectangle, opposite sides are equal, so the perimeter is length + width + length + width. We write this neatly as Perimeter = 2 × (length + width). For a square, all four sides are equal, so Perimeter = 4 × side length.

rules.title: Worked Example: Fencing a Vegetable Plot
rules.text: Let us work an example. Amina marks out a rectangular vegetable plot that is 5 m long and 3 m wide. Using the rule, Perimeter = 2 × (5 + 3) = 2 × 8 = 16 m. So she needs 16 metres of fencing to go all the way around. Now a square example: a square prayer mat has sides of 4 cm on a small model. Perimeter = 4 × 4 = 16 cm. Notice both answers came out as 16, but one is metres of fence and the other is centimetres of edge – always keep the unit attached to the number.

rules.title: Why Length × Width Gives the Area
rules.text: Why does length × width give the area? Imagine covering a rectangle with 1 cm squares. If the rectangle is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide, you can fit 6 squares along each row, and there are 4 rows. That is 6 × 4 = 24 little squares, so the area is 24 cm². Counting rows of squares is exactly what multiplication does quickly for us. This is why the rule for a rectangle is Area = length × width.

rules.title: Finding Missing Side Lengths
rules.text: The key skill for compound shapes is finding those missing side lengths. Here is the rule that never fails: opposite sides of the whole shape must balance. The lengths sticking up on one side must add to the same total as the tall side opposite them, and the same for the horizontal sides. Always draw the shape, label every length you are given, and then reason out the missing ones before you add or multiply. Rushing straight to the numbers is what causes mistakes here.

rules.title: Convert Units Before Calculating Area
rules.text: Here is a practical reason this matters. Idris measures a poster as 80 cm by 60 cm and wants its area in square metres. He can first convert the sides: 80 cm = 0.8 m and 60 cm = 0.6 m, then multiply: 0.8 × 0.6 = 0.48 m². Doing the conversion before multiplying often keeps the numbers tidy. The golden rule is simple: before you calculate area or perimeter, make sure all your measurements are in the same unit. Mixing metres and centimetres in one calculation is a certain path to a wrong answer.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Compound Shapes.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Most real shapes are not simple rectangles. A house floor plan, an L-shaped garden, or a swimming pool with a shallow end is a compound shape – a shape made by joining two or more simple shapes together. The good news is that you already have all the tools you need. The trick is to break the compound shape into simple rectangles, work out each one, and then combine them.

There are two methods for finding the area of a compound shape, and both are worth knowing. The addition method: split the shape into two or more rectangles, find each rectangle's area, and add them together. The subtraction method: imagine the shape as one big rectangle with a smaller rectangle removed, find both areas, and subtract the missing piece.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Estimating the Area of Irregular Shapes.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Not every shape is made of neat rectangles and triangles. The outline of a lake, a leaf, your own hand, or a country on a map is an irregular shape with curved or crooked edges. We cannot use a simple formula for these, but we can estimate the area very well by counting squares.

The method is called counting squares. Place the shape on a grid of squares, where each square is a known size such as 1 cm². Then count in two steps. First, count all the whole squares that lie completely inside the shape. Second, look at the part squares on the edge: if a part looks like about half a square or more, count it as one; if it looks like less than half, do not count it. Add the whole squares and the counted part squares together, and you have a good estimate of the area.

rounds.prompt: What does “Perimeter” mean?
choices: The distance around the outside edge of a shape
The amount of flat space inside a shape
A square one unit wide, used to measure area
The bottom side of a triangle / the straight distance up from it
rounds.answer: The distance around the outside edge of a shape
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 14 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Perimeter means The distance around the outside edge of a shape.

rounds.prompt: A rectangle is 6 cm wide and 7 cm tall. What is its perimeter in centimetres?
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.

rounds.prompt: A triangle has a base of 10 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is its area?
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 10 × 4 = 20 cm².

rounds.prompt: A rectangle is 4 cm wide and 14 cm tall. What is its area in square centimetres?
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.

selfAssessment: I can choose sensible units and convert between them (cm ↔ m, cm² ↔ m²).
I can solve real-world problems involving cost, materials, fencing and flooring.
I can explain the difference between perimeter (distance around) and area (space inside).
I can measure and calculate the perimeter of rectangles, squares, triangles and irregular shapes.
I can calculate the area of rectangles and squares using length × width.
I can calculate the area of a triangle using ½ × base × height.
I can find the area and perimeter of compound shapes by splitting or subtracting rectangles.
I can estimate the area of an irregular shape by counting whole and part squares.
I can use standard units of length, mass and capacity, convert between a larger and a smaller unit, and order a set of mixed-unit measurements.
I can round a measurement to the nearest whole unit, read and compare readings on different scales, and measure a line accurately to the nearest millimetre.
